questions.question: The architectural pattern that separates data, presentation, and logic.
questions.explanation: MVC divides applications into Model (data), View (UI), and Controller (business logic) for better organization.

questions.question: The design pattern that ensures only one instance of a class exists.
questions.explanation: Singleton pattern restricts a class to a single instance and provides global access to it.

questions.question: The design pattern that provides a simplified interface to a complex subsystem.
questions.explanation: Facade pattern offers a unified, simpler interface to a set of interfaces in a subsystem.

questions.question: The design pattern that allows incompatible interfaces to work together.
questions.explanation: Adapter pattern converts one interface into another that clients expect, enabling compatibility.

questions.question: The design pattern for creating objects without specifying their exact classes.
questions.explanation: Factory pattern provides an interface for creating objects without specifying concrete classes.

questions.question: The design principle stating each class should have one reason to change.
questions.explanation: SRP states that a class should have only one job or responsibility, making it easier to maintain.

questions.question: The design principle advocating not repeating code or knowledge.
questions.explanation: DRY principle emphasizes reducing repetition by abstracting common functionality.

questions.question: The measure of how related functions within a module are.
questions.explanation: Cohesion measures how closely related and focused the responsibilities of a module are.

questions.question: The degree of interdependence between software modules.
questions.explanation: Coupling measures how much one module depends on others; low coupling is preferable.

questions.question: An architectural style with independent, deployable services.
questions.explanation: Microservices architecture structures applications as collections of loosely coupled services.

questions.question: The design pattern that notifies all dependent objects when one object's state changes.
questions.explanation: The Observer pattern creates a one-to-many dependency so state changes automatically notify all subscribers.

questions.question: The design pattern acting as a placeholder that controls access to another object.
questions.explanation: The Proxy pattern provides a surrogate that controls access to another object for purposes like lazy loading or access control.

questions.question: The acronym for the design principle 'Keep It Simple, Stupid'.
questions.explanation: KISS reminds designers to favor simplicity, since simple designs are easier to build, test, and maintain.

questions.question: The creational pattern that creates new objects by cloning an existing instance.
questions.explanation: The Prototype pattern copies an existing instance to produce new objects, avoiding costly re-initialization.

questions.question: The UML diagram that depicts classes, their attributes, methods, and relationships.
questions.explanation: A Class Diagram models the static structure of a system, showing classes and associations between them.
